html:
The Xianbei were nomadic peoples of the eastern steppe, in today's Inner Mongolia and north east China, who took over the Mongolian steppe in the 2nd century CE and later ruled much of north China.

They came out of the old Donghu confederation, which the Xiongnu broke around 200 BCE. When Han armies and their southern Xiongnu allies crushed the northern Xiongnu around 90 CE, the Xianbei moved west into the empty steppe and took in many Xiongnu. Under the chief Tanshihuai, in the later 2nd century, they formed a short-lived steppe empire that raided the Han frontier.

In the Sixteen Kingdoms period after 304, Xianbei clans founded states inside China, such as the Yan kingdoms of the Murong clan. The Tuoba clan founded the Northern Wei, which united north China by 439. Its Emperor Xiaowen moved the capital to Luoyang in 494 and ordered his nobles to take Chinese names, dress and speech. On the steppe the Xianbei were replaced by the Rouran.

Xianbei families merged into the north Chinese elite. The ruling houses of the Sui and Tang dynasties married into Xianbei families and had Xianbei ancestors.
sum: The Xianbei were nomadic peoples of the eastern steppe, in today's Inner Mongolia and north east China, who took over the Mongolian steppe in the 2nd century CE and later ruled much of north China.
